messages.body_plain:
As I understand it, using acoustic indexes as relative measures of richness is more useful to compare between areas or recordings than as an absolute measure of a single site, as there is no direct connection between the values of the indices and the actual number of species (and mimic species would mess up any comparisons).

Entropy (H) (simplifying a lot)  measures where your sound sits between white noise (energy is equally distributed between all frequenciees, H = 0) and a pure tone ( energy is concentrated on a single frequency,  H=1). It does not measure species diversity, but  the distribution of energy across frequencies, and is severely affected by the amount of background noise in the recording, specially repetitive, anthropogenic noise. It can be correlated with species diversity if species occupy different frequencies in the soundscape, or have different temporal patterns. A complex pattern like birdsong would have values closer to 0.5 (or a bit higher than that) than to the extremes, as they are neither pure tones nor white noise, but structured in time and frequency. The values are not absolute measurements of diversity as there is no diversity when H =1 (you can check this by taking a file containing a pure tone, like A (440Hz) and calculating H on it, it should be very close to 1), but more useful when comparing sites and calls, as you can compare wheter areas are more or less diverse than each other (that is, energy is more or less spread out in different bands, due to the different structures of sounds)

Acoustic Richness Index takes the temporal entropy (Ht), and corrects it using the median of the amplitude envelope. This is supposed to correct for the background noise, as you said. However, it is also not an absolute measurement, and is actually caculated using ranked values for H and M, in different recordings. From the help file for AR():
AR = rank(M)*rank(Ht) / n^2
"As a ranked index, the results returned by AR strongly depends with the set of objects (respectively files) used as input. Comparaison between different data sets may be spurious. Computing AR on a set of a single object does not make any sense but is allowed. "

what this means is it calculates the indices for a set of recordings on the same site (or region, or day), and uses those recordings to calculate the diversity index AR for each area, ranked by the different energy distribution of the sound in each recording. Using it on a single file makes no sense, as the rank of the single recording would be 1, and no comparison would be possible. The more files you use, the bettter the comparisons will be, but the values will always be relative, not absolute, measures of diversity

Hope this helps,

messages.body_plain:
This is due to the time discretization of the STFT and an edge effect at the limits of the signal.
One way to limit this is to reduce the window size at the cost of frequency resolution (not very nice) :

library(tuneR)
library(seewave)

aa <- readWave("CT_48X2_start 17sec_amp.wav", units="seconds")
spectro(aa, ovlp=90, wn = "hamming", osc=TRUE, wl=256/4,
        flim=c(1, 4), tlim=c(1.61, 2.04),
        grid=FALSE, collevels=seq(-20,0,1))

The other solution is to add some silence before and after the sequence:

aa <- readWave("CT_48X2_start 17sec_amp.wav", from=1.61, to=2.04, units="seconds")
bb <- addsilw(aa, at="start", d=0.05, output="Wave")
cc <- addsilw(bb, at="end", d=0.05, output="Wave")
spectro(cc, ovlp=90, wn = "hamming", osc=TRUE, wl=256,
        flim=c(1, 4), grid=FALSE, collevels=seq(-20,0,1))

> As I understand it, using acoustic indexes as relative measures of richness is more useful to compare between areas or recordings than as an absolute measure of a single site, as there is no direct connection between the values of the indices and the actual number of species (and mimic species would mess up any comparisons).
>
> Entropy (H) (simplifying a lot)  measures where your sound sits between white noise (energy is equally distributed between all frequenciees, H = 0) and a pure tone ( energy is concentrated on a single frequency,  H=1). It does not measure species diversity, but  the distribution of energy across frequencies, and is severely affected by the amount of background noise in the recording, specially repetitive, anthropogenic noise. It can be correlated with species diversity if species occupy different frequencies in the soundscape, or have different temporal patterns. A complex pattern like birdsong would have values closer to 0.5 (or a bit higher than that) than to the extremes, as they are neither pure tones nor white noise, but structured in time and frequency. The values are not absolute measurements of diversity as there is no diversity when H =1 (you can check this by taking a file containing a pure tone, like A (440Hz) and calculating H on it, it should be very close to 1), but more useful when comparing sites and calls, as you can compare wheter areas are more or less diverse than each other (that is, energy is more or less spread out in different bands, due to the different structures of sounds)
>
> Acoustic Richness Index takes the temporal entropy (Ht), and corrects it using the median of the amplitude envelope. This is supposed to correct for the background noise, as you said. However, it is also not an absolute measurement, and is actually caculated using ranked values for H and M, in different recordings. From the help file for AR():
> AR = rank(M)*rank(Ht) / n^2
> "As a ranked index, the results returned by AR strongly depends with the set of objects (respectively files) used as input. Comparaison between different data sets may be spurious. Computing AR on a set of a single object does not make any sense but is allowed. "
>
> what this means is it calculates the indices for a set of recordings on the same site (or region, or day), and uses those recordings to calculate the diversity index AR for each area, ranked by the different energy distribution of the sound in each recording. Using it on a single file makes no sense, as the rank of the single recording would be 1, and no comparison would be possible. The more files you use, the bettter the comparisons will be, but the values will always be relative, not absolute, measures of diversity
>

> >

> > > As I understand it, using acoustic indexes as relative measures of richness is more useful to compare between areas or recordings than as an absolute measure of a single site, as there is no direct connection between the values of the indices and the actual number of species (and mimic species would mess up any comparisons).
> > >
> > > Entropy (H) (simplifying a lot)  measures where your sound sits between white noise (energy is equally distributed between all frequenciees, H = 0) and a pure tone ( energy is concentrated on a single frequency,  H=1). It does not measure species diversity, but  the distribution of energy across frequencies, and is severely affected by the amount of background noise in the recording, specially repetitive, anthropogenic noise. It can be correlated with species diversity if species occupy different frequencies in the soundscape, or have different temporal patterns. A complex pattern like birdsong would have values closer to 0.5 (or a bit higher than that) than to the extremes, as they are neither pure tones nor white noise, but structured in time and frequency. The values are not absolute measurements of diversity as there is no diversity when H =1 (you can check this by taking a file containing a pure tone, like A (440Hz) and calculating H on it, it should be very close to 1), but more useful when comparing sites and calls, as you can compare wheter areas are more or less diverse than each other (that is, energy is more or less spread out in different bands, due to the different structures of sounds)
> > >
> > > Acoustic Richness Index takes the temporal entropy (Ht), and corrects it using the median of the amplitude envelope. This is supposed to correct for the background noise, as you said. However, it is also not an absolute measurement, and is actually caculated using ranked values for H and M, in different recordings. From the help file for AR():
> > > AR = rank(M)*rank(Ht) / n^2
> > > "As a ranked index, the results returned by AR strongly depends with the set of objects (respectively files) used as input. Comparaison between different data sets may be spurious. Computing AR on a set of a single object does not make any sense but is allowed. "
> > >
> > > what this means is it calculates the indices for a set of recordings on the same site (or region, or day), and uses those recordings to calculate the diversity index AR for each area, ranked by the different energy distribution of the sound in each recording. Using it on a single file makes no sense, as the rank of the single recording would be 1, and no comparison would be possible. The more files you use, the bettter the comparisons will be, but the values will always be relative, not absolute, measures of diversity
> > >

> > > > > As I understand it, using acoustic indexes as relative measures of richness is more useful to compare between areas or recordings than as an absolute measure of a single site, as there is no direct connection between the values of the indices and the actual number of species (and mimic species would mess up any comparisons).
> > > > >
> > > > > Entropy (H) (simplifying a lot)  measures where your sound sits between white noise (energy is equally distributed between all frequenciees, H = 0) and a pure tone ( energy is concentrated on a single frequency,  H=1). It does not measure species diversity, but  the distribution of energy across frequencies, and is severely affected by the amount of background noise in the recording, specially repetitive, anthropogenic noise. It can be correlated with species diversity if species occupy different frequencies in the soundscape, or have different temporal patterns. A complex pattern like birdsong would have values closer to 0.5 (or a bit higher than that) than to the extremes, as they are neither pure tones nor white noise, but structured in time and frequency. The values are not absolute measurements of diversity as there is no diversity when H =1 (you can check this by taking a file containing a pure tone, like A (440Hz) and calculating H on it, it should be very close to 1), but more useful when comparing sites and calls, as you can compare wheter areas are more or less diverse than each other (that is, energy is more or less spread out in different bands, due to the different structures of sounds)
> > > > >
> > > > > Acoustic Richness Index takes the temporal entropy (Ht), and corrects it using the median of the amplitude envelope. This is supposed to correct for the background noise, as you said. However, it is also not an absolute measurement, and is actually caculated using ranked values for H and M, in different recordings. From the help file for AR():
> > > > > AR = rank(M)*rank(Ht) / n^2
> > > > > "As a ranked index, the results returned by AR strongly depends with the set of objects (respectively files) used as input. Comparaison between different data sets may be spurious. Computing AR on a set of a single object does not make any sense but is allowed. "
> > > > >
> > > > > what this means is it calculates the indices for a set of recordings on the same site (or region, or day), and uses those recordings to calculate the diversity index AR for each area, ranked by the different energy distribution of the sound in each recording. Using it on a single file makes no sense, as the rank of the single recording would be 1, and no comparison would be possible. The more files you use, the bettter the comparisons will be, but the values will always be relative, not absolute, measures of diversity

see the examples in the help files to see how you use the files path instead of the objects

setwd("C:/Documents")
oldNames<-list.files(getwd()))
nch=nchar(oldNames)
newNames<-paste0(substr(oldNames,1,nch-4),".wav")
for (i in 1:length(oldNames))
        file.rename(oldNames,newNames)

setwd("C:/Documents")
